This is something I've had to seriously think about recently given the legal threats and harassment my home business has been suffering this year. Frankly, I fear I would not survive long due to health problems, but I have long had an interest in nomadic lifestyles and mobile/portable shelter design. I understand that, for a small fee, many areas of public land allow for encampment for the span of one to a few months per year, leading to people who live nomadically, moving to different camp sites on a seasonal basis. Conventional RVs and trailers are incredibly overpriced but recently people have discovered the possibilities of contractors trailer or toy haulers'which are numerous and relatively cheap and can be converted into 'bug out' trailers and 'stealth campers' that are quite comfortable.

Traditional yurts are quite resilient mobile shelters suited to even harsh climate, though the larger ones are a bit heavy for transport and assembly by a solitary person. Surprisingly, they can be imported right from Mongolia for relatively low cost, from a few thousand dollars and up. There are now many dealers of these in the US as they have become quite popular with hippie-folk and as back yard yoga huts. More modern tent domes also make for good portable shelter and, in fact, differ from the traditional yurt mostly in the use of an alloy geodesic frame and more high-tech materials. The basic yurt architecture can be applied to a great variety of forms, structures, and materials and is potentially suited to structures based on CNC fabrication. I've long been interested in making a 'microyurt' that is based on puzzle-fit CNC cut weatboard using the 'calabash' form common to various kinds of furniture and some cat bed designs. I think this could be scaled to a comfortable small yurt size with integral couch, a Sunforger skin using pottery-like or native styled patterns and hosting a small vertical axis wind turbine on top to drive a heater for a round kotatsu and LED lighting. Rather like living in a high-tech genie bottle...

There are several contemporary 'neo-nomad' movements based on different approaches to nomadism created by our modern environments and technology. The simplest is known as just 'nomadism' or 'neo-nomadism', based largely on the kind of portable dwellings I noted above. In some cases the emphasis on travel is important and there is much exploration of the potential of bicycles as nomadic transport with the use of various kinds of bike trailers. There are many interesting designs these days for bike caravans often deriving from the classic teardrop trailer popular for small cars and motorcycles and long an attraction for DIY builders.

Then there is Urban Nomadism which is based on exploiting the potential of 'urban detritus'; the abandoned or underutilized buildings and spaces of the city and the various materials and other resources cast-off by businesses. By exploiting the urban infrastructure, the Urban Nomad relies on adaptive reuse of existing urban structures or man-portable micro-shelter that can be quickly deployed in many semi-sheltered urban settings and just as quickly packed and moved. The Urban Nomad is often an activist and his shelters may be used in a protest setting or he may be an urban interventionist, seeking to employ and share Maker skills on improving the quality of life and self-sufficiency of neighborhoods abandoned by the formal city government and market. Urban Nomadism relies heavily on the design and use of 'furnitecture' to facilitate rapid adaptive reuse. Furnitecture is a pet subject of mine and is basically a family of furniture design that bridges the line between furniture and architecture through the use of volumetric multi-funtional structures that define the purpose of space within and around them rather than relying on the use of fixed walls. Furnitecture and Urban Nomadism are closely linked by the work design Ken Isaacs and his explorations of Living Structures and Microhousing in the '60s and '70s. I've long been working on Nomadic Furnitecture concepts that combine rugged exteriors based on roadcase/flightcase construction with comfortable interior materials. For instance, I devised a pop-up sleeping pod that conceals a very traditional Japanese room complete with tatami mats and even tokonoma inside rough-and-ready roadcase packages that can fit through standard commercial doors. A project called Guerillaville that I've been developing seeks to use pods like this to create an indoor eco-village complete with urban farming systems that can be quick-deployed inside empty office buildings, warehouses, or parking structures.

Next is the Technomad, whose greatest example is Steven K. Roberts, the creator of the famous computer-equipped 'winnebiko' which traveled across the US in the 1980s. The Technomad's focus is a nomadic lifestyle seeking to push the limits of demote digital connectivity, relying on that connectivity and tech development as the basis of income.

Loosely related to this is the Digital Nomad who relies on Internet-related employment, such as programming, digital design, day-trading, or the like to support a cosmopolitan mobile lifestyle. Unlike the Technomad, the Digital Nomad relies on the pre-existing, and mostly urban, communications infrastructure for connectivity along with a host of supporting services like co-working centers, co-living situations, micro-apartments, and the other amenities of urban life to facilitate a very minimalist yet high-class mobile lifestyle where one's physical possessions are few and easily moved or digital in nature yet one's standard of living quite high.

Finally, there's Mobilism which is a concept originally proposed by Ken Isaacs as a means to reduce the environmental impact of daily life by employing seasonal mobility to reduce the energy overhead of maintaining comfort. We could much reduce our energy needs and save much money if we always lived in places where the climate was optimal, so we wouldn't have to heavily heat or cool our homes. But it's not practical to have whole homes in all these different places. So Isaacs proposed the division of the home between those elements that were too heavy to be moved--like infrastructure connections, foundations, and core structure--and those which could be made portable so that one would only need those few heavy elements in each place and easily move between them across the year. In the contemporary context Mobilism applies this strategy to a variety of open-plan structures designed to be hosts for Mobilist living. Like generic loft spaces specifically designed for quick outfitting and reconfiguration by plug-in furnitecture. You can imagine this as being like having an office partition systems designed for comfortable home living. They can be large urban buildings much like office buildings divided into many dwellings and many uses or simple free-standing pavilions for one home--like a park pavilion enclosed in window-walls. I've long planned to use this approach for my own home one day. Obviously, this approach to living requires the same kind of freedom of income as with the Digital Nomad but as we evolve toward a 'gig based' economy, this might become the norm for many people.
